title: Nucleus
summary: The membrane-bound compartment that holds the cell's DNA.

layers.basics: The nucleus is the cell's control room: it stores DNA and decides which genes are read.
layers.deeper: DNA is wrapped around histone proteins to form chromatin; pores in the double membrane control traffic.
layers.expert: In a typical human cell, ≈ 6.1×10^9 bp of DNA (diploid, ≈ 2 m end to end) is packed into a nucleus roughly 5-10 µm wide with roughly two thousand or more nuclear pores (the number varies with cell type and cell-cycle stage); the nuclear lamina supports the envelope; the nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosome subunits.

did_you_know: If you unwound the DNA from one human cell it would be about two meters long.

title: Mitochondrion
summary: The organelle that makes most of the cell's ATP.

layers.basics: Mitochondria burn fuel with oxygen to make ATP, the cell's energy currency.
layers.deeper: They have two membranes, and an inner membrane folded into cristae. They have their own small circular DNA.
layers.expert: Electron transport complexes I, III and IV pump protons across the inner membrane (complex II feeds electrons in from succinate without pumping); ATP synthase uses the proton gradient (≈ 150-180 mV); ≈ 16.6 kb mtDNA encoding 13 proteins; inherited almost always from the mother (rare paternal transmission has been reported and is debated).

facts: ≈ 30-32 (about 2 from glycolysis in the cytosol, the rest mitochondrial)
did_you_know: Mitochondria descend from bacteria that came to live inside an ancestral cell, well over a billion years ago. The exact date and the identity of the host cell are still debated.

title: Ribosome
summary: A molecular machine that builds proteins from instructions in mRNA.

layers.basics: Ribosomes read genetic messages and string amino acids together into proteins.
layers.deeper: They are made of RNA and protein and exist free or attached to the rough ER.
layers.expert: Mammalian 80S ribosome (60S + 40S) ≈ 4.3 MDa (yeast ≈ 3.3 MDa); the peptidyl transferase center is RNA-catalyzed (a ribozyme); amino acids are added at a few per second in eukaryotes (measured ≈ 3-10 per second in yeast) versus ≈ 12-21 per second in E. coli, depending on growth conditions.

did_you_know: The catalytic core of the ribosome is RNA, not protein.

title: Endoplasmic reticulum
summary: A network of membranes where many proteins are folded and modified as they are made, and where lipids are synthesised.

layers.basics: The ER is the cell's workshop: rough ER (studded with ribosomes) is where many new proteins enter and are folded; smooth ER makes fats and handles calcium.
layers.deeper: Rough ER is studded with ribosomes that feed new proteins through the Sec61 channel into the lumen; smooth ER lacks ribosomes, makes lipids, stores Ca2+ and, in liver, helps detoxify drugs. Together they can make up over half of a cell's membrane in some cell types.
layers.expert: Co-translational translocation via Sec61; N-glycosylation, disulfide formation, unfolded protein response; SR in muscle stores Ca2+.

facts: often ≈ 50% or more of a cell's total membrane (varies by cell type)
≈ 0.1-0.6 mM in reported measurements (varies with cell type and method), vs ≈ 0.05-0.1 µM in the cytosol at rest
did_you_know: In muscle cells a specialized ER called the sarcoplasmic reticulum stores the calcium that triggers contraction.

title: Golgi apparatus
summary: A stack of membrane sacs that sorts and ships proteins.

layers.basics: The Golgi puts final touches on proteins and packages them for delivery.
layers.deeper: Vesicles bud off carrying cargo to the cell surface or other organelles.
layers.expert: cis, medial and trans cisternae; glycan trimming and addition; lysosomal enzymes tagged with mannose-6-phosphate in the trans-Golgi network. How cargo crosses the stack is still debated: cisternae may mature and move forward, or vesicles may carry cargo between stable cisternae; most evidence favours maturation, possibly with tubular links.

facts: several per stack (number varies by cell type and organism)
did_you_know: It was discovered by Camillo Golgi in 1898 using a silver stain.
open_questions: Does cargo cross the Golgi by cisternal maturation, by vesicles hopping between stable cisternae, or by a mix that depends on cargo and cell type?

title: Lysosome
summary: An acidic recycling compartment containing digestive enzymes.

layers.basics: Lysosomes break down worn-out parts and swallowed germs.
layers.expert: Contain dozens of acid hydrolases (proteases, lipases, nucleases, glycosidases, sulfatases); V-ATPase acidifies; autophagy delivers cargo; lysosomal storage diseases arise mostly from deficient hydrolases, and some from defective lysosomal transporters or trafficking proteins.

did_you_know: In Tay-Sachs disease, a lack of the lysosomal enzyme hexosaminidase A lets a lipid (GM2 ganglioside) build up in nerve cells.

title: Peroxisome
summary: A small compartment that handles fatty-acid oxidation and neutralizes peroxides.

layers.basics: Peroxisomes break down certain fats and detoxify harmful by-products.
layers.deeper: They hold catalase to convert hydrogen peroxide to water.
layers.expert: β-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids; plasmalogen synthesis; Zellweger spectrum disorders.

did_you_know: Very-long-chain fatty acids are first shortened in peroxisomes, and the shorter products are then passed on to mitochondria.

title: Cell membrane
summary: A flexible oily barrier that surrounds every cell.

layers.basics: The membrane is a double layer of fat-like molecules that controls what enters and leaves.
layers.deeper: Proteins in it act as gates, pumps and receptors.
layers.expert: Fluid mosaic bilayer ≈ 4-5 nm thick for the lipids alone (oily core ≈ 3-4 nm); whole membranes with their proteins look thicker, roughly 7-10 nm, in electron micrographs; phospholipids and cholesterol (a large share, often tens of mol% in animal plasma membranes); transient lipid nanodomains ('rafts') whose size, lifetime and even existence in living cells remain debated; Na+/K+-ATPase uses a large share of a cell's ATP, with the fraction varying widely by cell type and highest in nerve cells.

facts: ≈ 5-10 nm (lipid bilayer ≈ 4-5 nm; ≈ 7-10 nm with proteins, in electron micrographs)
did_you_know: Scale a 10 µm cell up to a 10 m room and its ≈ 7.5 nm membrane would be about 7.5 mm thick.

title: Cytoskeleton
summary: A scaffold of protein filaments giving cells shape and movement.

layers.basics: Fibers inside the cell hold its shape and act as tracks for moving cargo.
layers.deeper: Actin filaments drive crawling and shape the cell cortex; intermediate filaments are rope-like and resist stretching; microtubules are hollow tubes that grow and shrink rapidly (dynamic instability) and serve as cargo tracks and as the mitotic spindle.
layers.expert: Actin ≈ 7 nm, intermediate ≈ 10 nm, microtubule ≈ 25 nm; motors kinesin and dynein walk on microtubules; myosin on actin.

did_you_know: Kinesin walks along microtubules with ≈ 8 nm steps, like a tiny two-legged robot.

title: Sarcomere
summary: The repeating contractile unit of striated muscle.

layers.basics: A sarcomere is a tiny stack of sliding filaments that shortens to generate force.
layers.deeper: Ca2+ binding to troponin uncovers myosin-binding sites on actin; myosin heads then bind, swing and release using ATP, pulling the thin filaments toward the M-line and the Z-discs together.
layers.expert: Skeletal muscle: isometric force is highest on a plateau at sarcomere lengths of about 2.05–2.2 µm (frog fibres, Gordon, Huxley and Julian 1966); the A-band (the length of a thick filament) is ≈ 1.85 µm in mammalian skeletal muscle; titin spans Z-disc to M-line. Force depends on how many myosin heads overlap thin filaments: it is highest on the plateau, falls at longer lengths as overlap is lost, and falls at lengths below about 1.67 µm.

facts: Length of peak force, skeletal muscle
Z-discs move closer together; the filaments keep their length
did_you_know: A single muscle fiber contains thousands of sarcomeres lined up end to end.
